'''Wen-yuan Qian''' ({{Lang-zh|t=錢文源}}; 14 April 1936 – 21 August 2003) was an American professor of history who taught at [[Blackburn College (Illinois)|Blackburn College]] and [[MacMurray College]].

== Early life and education ==

Qian was born in [[Shanghai]]. He studied physics at [[Peking University]], graduating in 1959.<ref name=":0" /> 

== Career ==
Qian taught physics at [[Zhejiang University]] from 1959 to 1980.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Obituary information for Wen-yuan Qian |url=https://www.airsman-hires.com/obituaries/Wen-yuan-Qian?obId=3446876 |access-date=2025-01-05 |website=www.airsman-hires.com |language=en-US |archive-date=2023-04-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401223539/https://www.airsman-hires.com/obituaries/Wen-yuan-Qian?obId=3446876 |url-status=live }}</ref> During the [[Cultural Revolution]], he was branded an "ideological counter-revolutionary."<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Henderson |first=John B. |date=1985 |title=Steps not Made |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |volume=230 |issue=4725 |pages=534–535 |doi=10.1126/science.230.4725.534 |issn=0036-8075 |jstor=1695246|pmid=17809681 }}</ref> In 1980, the [[government of the People's Republic of China]] sent Qian to the United States to continue his studies while his wife and daughter remained in China.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Cullen |first=Christopher |author-link=Christopher Cullen |date=1984-12-20 |title=Essays into history |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/312789b0.pdf |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |language=en |volume=312 |issue=5996 |pages=789–789 |doi=10.1038/312789a0 |issn=0028-0836}}</ref> In 1983, he graduated from [[Northwestern University]] with a [[Master of Arts]] in history.<ref name=":2" /> Qian was funded by the [[W. Clement Stone|W. Clement Stone Foundation]] to translate several works from Chinese to English.<ref name=":0" />

In 1985, Qian published his most known work, ''The Great Inertia: Scientific Stagnation in Traditional China''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cartier |first=Michel |date=August 1985 |title=Wen-yuan Qian, The Great Inertia: Scientific Stagnation in Traditional China, Londres-Sydney-Dover-New Hampshire, Croom Helm, 1984, XII + 155 p. |journal=[[Annales. Histoire, Sciences Sociales]] |language=fr |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=957–958 |doi=10.1017/S0395264900084432 |issn=0395-2649}}</ref> The work was framed as a challenge to [[Joseph Needham]]'s ''[[Science and Civilisation in China]],''<ref name=":1" /> and has been analyzed in relation to it.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gutmann |first=Matthew C. |date=January 1992 |title=Cross‐cultural conceits: Science in China and the West |journal=Science as Culture |language=en |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=208–239 |doi=10.1080/09505439209526345 |issn=0950-5431}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Daly |first=Jonathan |title=Historians Debate the Rise of the West |date=2014-07-11 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-1-317-68171-7 |edition= |pages=148 |language=en |chapter=Why not China? |doi=10.4324/9781315773537}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wang |first=Wensheng |date=March 2024 |title=The Value and Prospect of the Needham Question: A Historiographical Reflection and Elaboration |journal=[[Journal of World History]] |language=en |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=119–161 |doi=10.1353/jwh.2024.a920673 |issn=1527-8050}}</ref> He believed that political conditions, particularly the [[imperial examination]] system, stymied the development of modern science in dynastic China.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lin |first=Justin Yifu |author-link=Justin Yifu Lin |date=2008-01-01 |title=The Needham puzzle, the Weber question, and China's miracle: Long-term performance since the Sung dynasty |journal=China Economic Journal |language=en |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=63–95 |doi=10.1080/17538960701565053 |issn=1753-8963}}</ref> Qian saw the neglect of formal logic and rigorous proof as a central cause in the failure to develop modern science.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hannas |first=William C. |title=The Writing on the Wall: How Asian Orthography Curbs Creativity |date=2003-12-31 |publisher=[[University of Pennsylvania Press]] |isbn=978-0-8122-3711-5 |pages= |doi=10.9783/9780812202168 |ol=11345563M}}</ref>{{Rp|pages=108, 217}} At the time, Qian's thesis was considered controversial among [[Sinology|sinologists]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Mair |first=Victor H. |author-link=Victor H. Mair |date=October 1991 |title=Review |url=https://sino-platonic.org/complete/spp031_reviews.pdf |journal=[[Sino-Platonic Papers]] |publisher=[[University of Pennsylvania]] |issue=31}}</ref> [[Victor H. Mair]] called ''The Great Inertia'' an "arching cry of a thoughtful critic from within the Chinese tradition addressed to the enthusiastic advocate from without."<ref name=":3" />

In 1988, Qian graduated from the [[University of Michigan]] with a doctorate in history and began teaching history at [[Blackburn College (Illinois)|Blackburn College]] the same year. From 1992 to 2002, he taught history at [[MacMurray College]].<ref name=":0" /> Qian died in 2003 in [[Jacksonville, Illinois]].<ref name=":0" />
